chapters.title: Protection from Above
chapters.sourcePressure: Uses the Johnny Bravo rescue frame to define leadership as cover from above: power becomes useful when it moves toward exposed people, with empathy making their danger real enough to act on.
chapters.coreMove: Convert authority into visible cover by absorbing the first risk before asking exposed people to be brave.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating safety as praise, niceness, or removing standards instead of spending authority to reduce avoidable fear.

chapters.title: Employees Are People Too
chapters.sourcePressure: Moves from factory-bell control to the claim that employees are not process attachments. Humane recognition is operational because dignity changes judgment, candor, and responsibility.
chapters.coreMove: Replace process-first control with one humanizing question that restores dignity before judging performance.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the chapter to be nicer to staff while leaving the system blind to context and dignity.

chapters.title: Belonging
chapters.sourcePressure: Defines belonging as durable membership inside the Circle of Safety, where people stop treating hard moments as possible exile and become more candid under pressure.
chapters.coreMove: Turn inclusion from roster status into durable membership by proving one mistake will not eject someone from the group.
chapters.commonMisread: Making belonging mean warmth, similarity, or social events rather than secure membership with standards intact.

chapters.title: Yeah, But...
chapters.sourcePressure: Tests practical objections to safety-first leadership and separates useful constraints from excuse language that preserves blame, distance, or social threat.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a yeah-but objection into a design constraint instead of letting it excuse fear-based behavior.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating every objection as cynicism, or treating pressure as proof that safety is unrealistic.

chapters.title: When Enough Is Enough
chapters.sourcePressure: Introduces sufficiency as a leadership judgment: more can keep sounding responsible after the original need is met, and pursuit can slip its purpose.
chapters.coreMove: Name the sufficiency line before more starts impersonating responsibility.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into anti-ambition or simple moderation instead of judging when pursuit detaches from purpose.

chapters.title: E.D.S.O.
chapters.sourcePressure: Frames culture as reward design through endorphins, dopamine, serotonin, and oxytocin, warning that fast solo payoff can thin out trust.
chapters.coreMove: Audit which internal reward your system overfeeds and rebalance quick wins with trust-building rewards.
chapters.commonMisread: Overexplaining brain chemistry or treating chemicals as destiny instead of using them as a leadership lens for reward patterns.

chapters.title: The Big C
chapters.sourcePressure: Isolates the chronic alarm force that keeps people braced, making truth, trust, and cooperation bend toward self-protection.
chapters.coreMove: Find the chronic threat signal in the room and remove one source of permanent alarm before asking for candor.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating pressure itself as bad, or diagnosing individual anxiety while ignoring environmental signals.

chapters.title: Why We Have Leaders
chapters.sourcePressure: Answers why groups need leaders: authority exists to preserve safety, trusted networks, and steadiness when strain rises, with burden before privilege.
chapters.coreMove: Use rank as a burden-bearing function before claiming any privilege attached to it.
chapters.commonMisread: Making leadership a title, charisma trait, or meal-time symbol instead of a protective function.

chapters.title: The Courage to Do the Right Thing
chapters.sourcePressure: Turns leadership into cost: courage is accepting discomfort or risk so people, truth, and standards are not abandoned under pressure.
chapters.coreMove: Choose the costly right action that sends burden toward you instead of down the chain.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating courage as personal boldness, dramatic confrontation, or risk for its own sake.

chapters.title: Snowmobile in the Desert
chapters.sourcePressure: Uses the snowmobile metaphor to diagnose fit before blame: poor performance may reveal a mismatch between human design, conditions, incentives, and environment.
chapters.coreMove: Diagnose the terrain before you label the person as defective.
chapters.commonMisread: Excusing all underperformance as environmental or turning fit into a personality-matching exercise.

chapters.title: The Boom Before the Bust
chapters.sourcePressure: Warns that successful periods can normalize habits and structures that later become failure mechanisms; strong results can postpone diagnosis.
chapters.coreMove: Read a boom for the hidden habits it is teaching before success makes them untouchable.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the boom as simple greed, luck, or macroeconomic history instead of cultural training during success.

chapters.title: The Boomers All Grown Up
chapters.sourcePressure: Shows how boom-era institutional training becomes adult leadership expectation, making inherited rules feel timeless and personal clashes look like character problems.
chapters.coreMove: Trace a leadership norm back to the era that rewarded it before treating resistance as attitude.
chapters.commonMisread: Blaming a generation or defending another generation instead of seeing historical training inside institutions.

chapters.title: Abstraction Kills
chapters.sourcePressure: Names abstraction as the danger of distance: people become units, functions, or reports, letting harmful choices feel professional because the human cost is unseen.
chapters.coreMove: Reattach a name, face, and consequence to any category before letting the category decide.
chapters.commonMisread: Claiming all models, rules, or numbers are bad, rather than showing when distance replaces responsibility.

chapters.title: Modern Abstraction
chapters.sourcePressure: Extends abstraction into modern scale, metrics, and systems: tools create clarity while widening the gap between authority and consequence.
chapters.coreMove: Use modern systems as lenses while adding a deliberate return path to lived reality.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into anti-technology or anti-scale instead of managing the distance modern tools create.

chapters.title: Managing the Abstraction
chapters.sourcePressure: Turns abstraction into discipline: reports, rules, and categories remain useful only when leaders reconnect them to lived human consequence before judgment hardens.
chapters.coreMove: Pause the process at the point where it would close and reopen contact with the human consequence underneath.
chapters.commonMisread: Making this a generic balanced leadership chapter, or rejecting processes rather than keeping them subordinate to judgment.

chapters.title: Imbalance
chapters.sourcePressure: Names the crowding-out pattern where measurable order gains authority over less visible but essential human conditions like trust, discretion, and judgment.
chapters.coreMove: Detect the side of the system being overfed and deliberately support the human condition being crowded out.
chapters.commonMisread: Complaining that metrics are cold, or calling every workload problem imbalance.

chapters.title: Leadership Lesson 1: So Goes the Culture, So Goes the Company
chapters.sourcePressure: Makes culture causal: the company becomes what people learn to repeat under pressure from signals, rewards, tolerated tradeoffs, and protected behavior.
chapters.coreMove: Read culture from repeated pressure behaviors, then change the signal people are copying.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing culture to morale, values statements, or atmosphere instead of a repeated learning system.

chapters.title: Leadership Lesson 2: So Goes the Leader, So Goes the Culture
chapters.sourcePressure: Shows leader behavior as upstream cultural instruction: what authority models, protects, excuses, and punishes teaches the group how the place works.
chapters.coreMove: Treat your visible reaction under pressure as the lesson the culture will copy.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the lesson about personality, inspiration, or speeches instead of observed conduct.

chapters.title: Leadership Lesson 3: Integrity Matters
chapters.sourcePressure: Defines integrity as coherence under pressure: principles remain real in costly cases or the culture learns that exceptions and excuses outrank standards.
chapters.coreMove: Keep the stated principle intact at the first costly exception where everyone is watching.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating integrity as private sincerity, reputation, or honesty in easy cases.

chapters.title: Leadership Lesson 4: Friends Matter
chapters.sourcePressure: Treats friendship as operational loyalty: people behave differently when known and valued by actual people instead of reduced to roles, metrics, or incentives.
chapters.coreMove: Build enough real mutual knowledge that candor and sacrifice have a relationship to travel through.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning friendship into favoritism, forced fun, or social softness detached from fairness and honesty.

chapters.title: Leadership Lesson 5: Lead the People, Not the Numbers
chapters.sourcePressure: Attacks the substitution error in abstraction: numbers are clues, not commanders, and should direct leaders toward people and context beneath the signal.
chapters.coreMove: Use the number to find the people, then let human context govern the decision.
chapters.commonMisread: Rejecting metrics or worshiping empathy while ignoring that numbers can reveal real pressure.

chapters.title: At the Center of All Our Problems Is Us
chapters.sourcePressure: Argues for implicated participation: systems matter, but ordinary choices for convenience, silence, short-term relief, and compromise keep reproducing the culture people criticize.
chapters.coreMove: Replace system blame with one implicated habit you personally keep feeding.
chapters.commonMisread: Collapsing structural critique into personal blame, or using systems as an alibi for passivity.

chapters.title: At Any Expense
chapters.sourcePressure: Warns that visible success becomes morally thin when the human bill is hidden, delayed, or displaced onto less visible people.
chapters.coreMove: Refuse to call a win clean until you have found who pays the hidden bill.
chapters.commonMisread: Making this anti-performance or ignoring hard tradeoffs instead of exposing displaced cost.

chapters.title: The Abstract Generation
chapters.sourcePressure: Frames generation as formation under abstract conditions of belonging, approval, progress, and consequence, calling for concrete trust rather than stereotype.
chapters.coreMove: Diagnose the conditions that formed a thin-trust habit before judging it as attitude.
chapters.commonMisread: Stereotyping millennials or any generation, or excusing all behavior as formation.

chapters.title: Step 12
chapters.sourcePressure: Frames change as recovery process: destructive leadership habits require admission, repeated practice, accountability, and help, not isolated insight.
chapters.coreMove: Turn insight about a harmful habit into a repeatable recovery process with accountability.
chapters.commonMisread: Borrowing recovery language as metaphor only, or treating admission as the whole change.

chapters.title: Shared Struggle
chapters.sourcePressure: Shows that difficulty deepens trust when burden is mutual, visible, and protected, while rejecting abuse, arbitrary harshness, and outsourced strain.
chapters.coreMove: Enter the burden with others so the cost becomes mutual instead of displaced.
chapters.commonMisread: Romanticizing suffering, hazing, or hardship as inherently bonding.

chapters.title: We Need More Leaders
chapters.sourcePressure: Closes by distributing leadership: humane institutions need more people taking local responsibility for protection and human cost instead of waiting for titles above them.
chapters.coreMove: Take local responsibility for the human cost near you before hierarchy gives you permission.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling for more managers, more charismatic leaders, or heroic lone saviors.
